title: We Are Not as Rational as We Think
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 together. The bat costs a dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? If “ten cents” flashed through your mind, you answered like most people, including students at the best universities. And you got it wrong, because then the total would be $1.20. The ball costs five cents. The most interesting part is that the wrong answer came instantly, with a full sense of obviousness.

The mind runs in two gears. The fast gear recognizes faces and hits the brakes, but it quietly swaps hard questions for easy ones: instead of “Will this candidate make a good director?” it answers “Does he look confident?” The slow gear calculates and weighs things, but it’s lazy. That’s where a whole gallery of illusions comes from: the first number we hear pulls our judgments along with it, which is why “marked down from $399 to $199” works better than the price alone. We fear sharks and planes, not stairs and the drive to the airport, because what seems dangerous is whatever is spectacular. We let in information that agrees with our views without checking it. We stick with failing projects because “we’ve already put so much into it.” And the vast majority of drivers consider themselves better than the majority of drivers, which mathematically cannot be true.

The worst part is that knowing about these traps doesn’t switch them off: they work like optical illusions, and even the people who study them fall for them. What does help is procedures: make important decisions well rested; do the math on paper, not in your head; ask what would have to be true for you to be wrong; imagine that your decision has turned out to be a disaster, and tell the story of what went wrong. With bigger purchases, wait three days and see whether the desire survived, because a crossed-out price and a countdown timer were working on it. Don’t make decisions hungry or tired either, because even experts at the end of a long day choose what’s easier, not what’s better. And ask others to take a look, because other people’s eyes see your blind spots.

Psychology has measured what the book of Proverbs wrote down long ago: there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death. Since our own judgment misleads us, it’s wise to lean on something outside ourselves.

quote.text: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight.

questions: In what matter would it be worth allowing yourself the thought today: “I could be wrong”?
Whom do you really ask for advice when making important decisions?

paragraphs: A simple puzzle: a bat and a ball cost $1.10 together. The bat costs a dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? If “ten cents” flashed through your mind, you’re in very large company: that’s the answer most people give, including most students at the best universities in the world. And it’s the wrong answer. If the ball cost ten cents, the bat would cost $1.10, and together they would come to $1.20. The ball costs five cents. What’s interesting about this puzzle isn’t the solution itself, but what we felt for a moment: the wrong answer came instantly, effortlessly, and with a full sense of obviousness.

That is exactly how the mind works. It has what amounts to two gears. The first is fast and automatic: it recognizes faces, hits the brakes, and serves up ready-made judgments in a split second. The second is slow and costly: it calculates, compares, and weighs arguments, but it requires concentration, so it kicks in reluctantly. For most of the day the fast gear is in charge, and thank goodness, because without it we couldn’t even cross the street. The trouble is that the fast mind, brilliant in a thousand matters, gets things systematically wrong in certain situations, and we believe it, because its suggestions come with a feeling of certainty. Its favorite trick is swapping the question: instead of the hard question “Will this candidate make a good director?” it quietly answers the easier one, “Does he look self-assured?” Instead of “Is this investment sensible?” it answers “Is the person offering it to me likable?”

This machinery gives rise to a whole gallery of illusions that psychology has been measuring and cataloging for half a century. Anchoring: the first number we hear pulls all our subsequent judgments along with it, even if it’s random. That’s why a tag reading “marked down from $399 to $199” works better than the $199 price alone, and why whoever names a figure first in a negotiation sets the terms of the whole conversation. Availability: we judge as common and dangerous whatever is easy to call to mind. After every shark movie we’re afraid of the sea, even though the stairs at home are far more dangerous; we fear the flight, not the drive to the airport, even though the statistics say the opposite. Confirmation: we let in information that agrees with our beliefs without checking it, and send contradicting information back for revision. We read authors who agree with us, and a year later our view is firmer, though not a bit truer. Sunk costs: we stick with the wrong college major, projects, and TV series because “we’ve already put so much into it,” even though no one will give back what we put in, and all that counts is what lies ahead. Loss aversion: a loss hurts roughly twice as much as an equal gain pleases, so we cling to things we should have gotten rid of long ago. Then there’s survivorship bias: we see those who gave up everything and won, because the losers don’t give interviews, so we badly overestimate our chances of following in their footsteps. Then there’s the halo effect: we reflexively credit a good-looking, self-assured person with competence and honesty, even though looks have nothing to do with either, which is why a well-cut suit can stand in for arguments. The narrative fallacy: a smooth, coherent story seems truer to us than dry statistics, so a single moving story persuades us more than a thousand cases that say otherwise. And finally overconfidence, the illusion of illusions: the vast majority of drivers consider themselves better than the majority of drivers, which mathematically cannot be true.

On top of that, our judgments sway along with our bodies. Mood, hunger, and fatigue really do change decisions, and not just among amateurs: researchers have shown that professional experts, from doctors to officials, more often choose the easier option rather than the better one at the end of a long day. The same person, with the same knowledge, decides one way in the morning and another way after ten hours of work. If that’s the case, the time of day you make a decision is not a detail. It’s part of the decision.

Our forecasts deserve a chapter of their own. Nearly every renovation takes longer and costs more than planned, nearly every “two-week” project takes a month, and even though we’ve lived through this dozens of times, we plan for the thirty-first time with the same optimism. That’s because the mind plans the ideal scenario, in which no one gets sick, nothing breaks, and nothing arrives late, and life doesn’t play out that way. The practical fix is simple: don’t ask yourself how long it will take; check how long it took others who did something similar, and add a buffer.

And now for the truly uncomfortable news: knowing about these traps doesn’t switch them off. They work like optical illusions. You can know for certain that two lines are equal, measure them with a ruler, and one will still look longer. The very people who study these traps professionally fall into them. Our minds simply work the way they work, and no amount of reading will change that. What we can change is something else: the procedures by which we make important decisions.

Here are a few procedures worth putting into practice. First, sort your decisions into small ones and big ones. Make the small ones quickly and without regret, because they aren’t worth the slow gear. With the big ones, such as a job, a home, a major purchase, or an important conversation, deliberately slow down: sleep on the decision, and do the math on paper instead of estimating in your head, because writing engages the slow gear of the mind. Second, actively look for counterarguments. Ask yourself what would have to be true for you to be wrong, and ask someone you trust to play devil’s advocate for fifteen minutes. It’s unpleasant and priceless. Third, hold a dress rehearsal of failure: imagine it’s a year from now and your decision has turned out to be a flop, and now tell the story of what went wrong. This simple exercise uncovers risks that enthusiasm didn’t want to see. Fourth, don’t make important decisions when you’re hungry, tired, or in the grip of strong emotions, because mood and fatigue really do change the rulings even of professional experts. And fifth, use other people’s eyes. Other people aren’t smarter than you, but they have one advantage: they aren’t inside your head, so they can see your blind spots. The book of Proverbs put this principle briefly: with many counselors comes deliverance.

In everyday life, one more simple rule comes in handy, especially with money: put off the purchase. With bigger expenses, wait three days from the moment of “I have to have it” and see whether the desire survived. Usually it doesn’t, because it was fueled by anchoring on a crossed-out price, a countdown saying “offer ends in two hours,” and free shipping on orders over $200, for the sake of which you toss $80 worth of extra stuff into your cart. Stores employ people who know everything about your illusions. It makes sense to know at least a little about them yourself.

There is one more benefit to all this knowledge, quieter and deeper. Anyone who has once seen how easily their own mind produces certainty without backing looks at disagreements differently. They are more careful with sentences that begin with “I’m sure.” They more readily allow for the thought that this time the right answer may be on the other side of the table. In a family quarrel and in an online brawl, after all, both sides have the same sense of obviousness that told you “ten cents” in the bat-and-ball puzzle. Simply remembering that ball in the middle of an argument is often the cheapest lesson in humility there is. Intellectual humility is not a weakness of thinking. It is its highest form.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: The mind runs in two gears: a fast one, which serves up instant judgments with a sense of certainty, and a slow one, which calculates and weighs but is lazy. The fast gear goes wrong systematically, in predictable ways: it anchors on the first number, fears what is spectacular rather than what is common, looks for confirmation of its own beliefs, defends sunk costs, falls for good looks and smooth stories, and overrates its own abilities. On top of that, decisions sway along with the body: hunger, fatigue, and the time of day change choices even among experts. Knowing about these traps doesn’t switch them off, just as knowing about an optical illusion doesn’t straighten the picture. What does help is procedures: make important decisions well rested and on paper, actively look for counterarguments, imagine your own failure in advance and ask what led to it, wait three days before bigger purchases, and above all, ask others to take a look, because other people’s eyes see your blind spots.

sections.heading: Look Higher
paragraphs: It’s amusing and a little touching: psychology has spent millions on research to measure something the book of Proverbs wrote down in a single verse, that there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death. The Bible has long treated the human heart with a tender distrust: it knows the heart can deceive itself, and that’s why it so often warns against being wise in one’s own eyes. But it doesn’t leave us with the diagnosis alone. Since our own judgment can be deceptive, wisdom means leaning on something outside ourselves: on the Word, which doesn’t change its mind depending on our mood; on a community that sees our blind spots; on prayer, in which a person stops being the only judge of his own plans. “Lean not on your own understanding” is not a call to mindlessness. It is the most rational sentence you can say to a being whose mind produces certainty faster than truth.

quote.text: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight. Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil.

questions: In what matter could your self-confidence be your greatest danger today?
Whom do you ask for advice when making important decisions, and to whom do you only defend decisions you’ve already made?
What would “lean not on your own understanding” mean for you in practice when you face your next important decision?
